record.paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
record.original_question: Which flare properties, including total energy, event frequency, emitted spectrum, and spectral distribution, most strongly control exoplanet atmospheric chemistry and photochemistry, and can those controlling properties be inferred observationally from extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy, imaging, or X-ray data?

evidence.quote: • Which ﬂare properties (energy, frequency, emissions, spectral distribution) most inﬂuence exoplanet atmospheres and photochemistry, and can these properties be inferred using techniques such as EUV spectroscopy and imaging or x-ray data? [85, 86]

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a host star that emits stellar flares, where each flare event is characterized by: (i) its bolometric energy E (in erg), (ii) the occurrence-rate (frequency) distribution dN/dE governing how often flares of a given energy occur per unit time, (iii) the emitted electromagnetic spectrum F(λ, t) describing the wavelength- and time-resolved radiative output, and (iv) the spectral energy distribution describing how flare energy is partitioned across wavelengths (in particular among extreme-ultraviolet (EUV), far-ultraviolet (FUV), near-ultraviolet (NUV), optical, and X-ray bands). Suppose an orbiting planet has an atmosphere whose composition evolves under a coupled photochemical–chemical kinetic model driven by the time-dependent stellar irradiation, including photolysis rates that depend on F(λ, t) and on cumulative fluence in each band.

(a) Identify, within this framework, which of the flare properties E, dN/dE, F(λ, t), and the band-resolved spectral energy distribution exert the dominant control on the steady-state and transient photochemical composition of the planetary atmosphere; quantify the relative sensitivity of major atmospheric chemical species (e.g., O3, H2O, CH4, CO2, NOx, HOx) to each property.

(b) Determine whether the controlling flare properties identified in (a) — in particular the EUV spectral energy distribution F_EUV(λ, t), which is largely unobservable directly for stars other than the Sun due to interstellar absorption — can be reconstructed from observable proxies, namely: EUV spectroscopy where available, EUV/UV imaging, and X-ray spectra and light curves. Specifically, establish whether there exists a reliable inversion or scaling relation mapping observed X-ray and UV/EUV imaging/spectral diagnostics to the flare property (or properties) most relevant for driving exoplanet atmospheric photochemistry, and characterize its uncertainty.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a forward-looking open research question in heliophysics/exoplanet science. No published work establishes a definitive ranking of flare properties controlling exoplanet atmospheric chemistry, nor a validated inversion from X-ray/EUV imaging to the EUV spectral energy distribution that drives photochemistry; current literature (e.g., MUSCLES, HAZMAT, and recent flare-photochemistry modeling) provides partial constraints but no consensus answer.

status_evidence.title: MUSCLES Treasury Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Reconstructed EUV spectra of M and K dwarfs from FUV/X-ray proxies, with substantial modeling uncertainty.
status_evidence.claim: EUV reconstruction relies on indirect proxies and remains uncertain, indicating the inversion problem is not solved.

status_evidence.title: Loyd et al., HAZMAT/MUSCLES flare studies
status_evidence.snippet: UV flare energy distributions on M dwarfs and their potential photochemical impact on planetary atmospheres are characterized statistically but with limited EUV coverage.
status_evidence.claim: Flare photochemical impact has been studied but the dominant controlling property has not been definitively established.
